title: Managing Secrets for AI Agents
summary: Four ways to hold an agent's credential, and what a leak costs under each. Cryptoperiods from NIST SP 800-57, Vault leases, rotation that survives a running workflow, and why revoking is two steps.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Most agent secret failures are not sophisticated attacks. They are a credential sitting somewhere it was never supposed to reach, with no expiry date on it.**


Google says of its own key format that service-account keys "don't have an expiry time and stay valid until you delete them", and that holding the private key "is similar to knowing a user's password". MITRE rates hard-coded credentials, CWE-798, as High likelihood of exploit, partly because the password "usually cannot be changed or disabled by system administrators without manually modifying the program".


The common framing treats a secret as plumbing, wired once and forgotten. For an agent that is backwards. The secret *is* the blast radius: whatever the credential reaches, the agent reaches, on its own initiative, at any hour.


We are not claiming more approval steps would help. A narrower door and a shorter clock would. NIST's key-management guidance exists precisely to bound how long a compromise stays useful.


Start with two changes. Give every agent credential an expiry, even an arbitrary one, so that "forever" stops being the default. And make the agent's reasoning loop unable to read the raw value, because the moment it can, the value is in a transcript.
